title: Human Approval Gates: The Line Between Demo and Product
linkedin_md:
# Human Approval Gates: The Line Between Demo and Product

A demo agent can take bold actions because the blast radius is fake.

A production agent cannot.

That is the line a lot of LLM systems cross too casually. The model drafts an email, updates a record, closes a ticket, changes permissions, issues a refund, deletes data, or triggers a workflow. In the demo, this feels like magic. In production, it is an incident waiting for the right prompt, stale context, bad retrieval result, or ambiguous instruction.

The difference between a useful agent and a dangerous one is not whether it can act. It is whether the system knows which actions require human approval.

[YOUR STORY HERE - 2-3 paragraphs]

## Irreversible Is The Wrong Word, But The Right Instinct

Very few actions are truly irreversible.

You can often send a correction email. You can restore a database row. You can reopen a ticket. You can reverse a payment. You can roll back a config change.

But users do not experience these as reversible. They experience them as trust breaks.

A better practical definition:

An action needs approval if undoing it is expensive, visible, compliance-sensitive, destructive, or socially awkward.

That includes:

- Sending messages to external people
- Moving money or credits
- Changing access permissions
- Deleting or overwriting user data
- Submitting forms or applications
- Publishing content
- Closing support, legal, financial, or operational workflows
- Making commitments on behalf of a person or organization

The common failure mode is treating all tool calls the same. Search, summarize, draft, classify, and mutate are not in the same risk class.

A model reading data is one thing. A model changing the world is another.

## The Approval Gate Is Part Of The Product

A human approval gate should not feel like a modal slapped on after the agent is done.

It is part of the workflow design.

The user should understand:

- What the agent is about to do
- What data it used
- What will change
- Who will see the result
- Whether it can be undone
- What the alternatives are

Bad approval UI says:

> Approve action?

Good approval UI says:

> Send this email to 3 external recipients using the draft below. It references the pricing terms from the uploaded contract and will attach the generated PDF.

That second version gives the human a real chance to catch the error.

The approval step is not just a checkbox for safety. It is the moment where the system transfers agency back to the user.

## Use Risk Tiers, Not Vibes

A simple tiering model works better than long debates about autonomy.

Tier 0: Read-only  
The agent can search, retrieve, inspect, summarize, classify, and answer. No approval needed beyond normal access control.

Tier 1: Draft-only  
The agent can prepare artifacts, but cannot submit them. Examples: email drafts, report drafts, database update previews, proposed config changes.

Tier 2: Reversible internal actions  
The agent can make low-risk changes inside a controlled system. Examples: tagging records, assigning labels, creating internal notes, updating non-critical metadata. Log everything. Allow easy undo.

Tier 3: External or consequential actions  
The agent must ask for approval. Examples: sending external messages, changing permissions, issuing refunds, publishing pages, filing forms, deleting records.

Tier 4: High-stakes actions  
The agent should require stronger controls: multi-party approval, step-up authentication, rate limits, policy checks, or no automation at all. Examples: large financial movement, legal commitments, security changes, production infrastructure changes, regulated workflows.

This does not need to be perfect on day one. Even a coarse four-tier policy is better than letting every tool call run because the demo looked smooth.

## Approval Gates Need Context Windows Too

One subtle issue: approval gates often show the final output, but not the reasoning context.

That is not enough.

If the model proposes a refund, show the order, the policy excerpt, the user request, and the calculated amount.

If the model proposes an outbound email, show the recipient list, attachments, source facts, and any uncertain claims.

If the model proposes a permission change, show current access, new access, affected resources, and expiry if there is one.

The human should not have to reconstruct the situation from scratch. If reviewing takes longer than doing the task manually, the gate will be bypassed, ignored, or rubber-stamped.

A useful target: approval should take 5 to 15 seconds for common actions, and 30 to 90 seconds for higher-risk actions.

Past that, you probably need a better summary, better diff, or a narrower action.

## The Agent Should Know When It Is Asking

Do not make approval a generic final step.

The agent should be trained or programmed to recognize risk boundaries during planning.

For example:

1. Gather context
2. Decide intended action
3. Classify action risk
4. If approval required, produce a review packet
5. Wait for explicit approval
6. Execute exactly the approved action
7. Log result

The important part is step 6: execute exactly the approved action.

A common bug is letting the model regenerate the action after approval. The user approved version A, but the agent sends version B because the context changed, the model sampled differently, or another tool result appeared.

Approval should freeze the payload.

If the approved email body, recipient list, amount, record ID, or permission set changes, approval is invalidated.

## Logs Are Not A Substitute For Gates

Audit logs are useful after something goes wrong.

Approval gates prevent some things from going wrong in the first place.

You want both.

For every consequential action, log:

- User instruction
- Model output
- Tool call payload
- Approval timestamp
- Approver identity
- Final executed payload
- External response or confirmation
- Any policy checks applied

This is not just for compliance. It is for debugging.

When a user says, "Why did it do that?", you need an answer better than "the model decided."

## The Product Question

The hard product question is not "Can the agent do this?"

It is:

Should the agent do this without asking?

That question decides whether you are building a production system or a very impressive demo.

Demos optimize for flow. Products optimize for trust.

Demos hide friction. Products put friction in the right place.

Demos show what is possible. Products define what is allowed.

[YOUR STORY HERE - 2-3 paragraphs]

## Takeaways

Human approval gates are not a lack of ambition. They are how you ship agentic systems into environments where mistakes matter.

Start with read-only and draft-only flows. Add low-risk reversible actions once logging and undo are solid. Put explicit approval in front of anything external, destructive, financial, permission-changing, or commitment-making.

Freeze the approved payload. Show the human the actual diff. Keep approval fast enough that people use it. Log enough that you can explain what happened later.

The agent does not need full autonomy to be valuable.

It needs the right autonomy, bounded by the real cost of being wrong.
